Behaviors related to purchase, use and disposal of goods and services have a direct effect on the environment. Researchers related recycling behavior to the environmental concern of people, and Schultz and Oskamp (1996) found that the amount of effort consumers were willing to exert to recycle moderated the relationship between attitudes of environmental concern and recycling. Recycling, in general, was perceived as an easier environmental behavior (Green-Demeirs, Pelletier, & M enard, 1997), and thus, likely to be performed more often. Recycling behavior can be understood well from the two constructs: general attitude toward recycling (includes the importance of recycling), and the specific attitude toward the inconvenience of recycling (Akil et al., 2015; McCarty & Shrum, 2001). It was also highlighted by early researchers that recycling was motivated by factors other than personal convenience. However, Vining and Ebreo (1992) have shown that curbside recycling behavior was different from other forms of recycling behaviors. Recycling, by itself, is a resource-recovery mechanism, whereas waste minimization leads to lesser usage of these valuable resources. Though both of them are sustainable behaviors, waste minimization and recycling have widely differing antecedents (Barr, 2003). Ebreo and Vining (2001) agreed to Barr’s view about these differences. Incentives and barriers to adopting these behaviors have been studied by Garc es et al. (2002), and Tucker and Speirs (2003). Bratt (1999) studied different environmental behaviors and concluded that consumers did not have a generalized behavior; they behaved differently with respect to different product categories. The differentiation and generalization of predictors of these behaviors are crucial for the sustainability concerns of researchers and policy makers.

It is also observed that though the articles give considerable input to the awareness on recycling behavior, the prime focus of the leading studies in the cluster is ‘waste minimization’. According to Tonglet et al. (2004a), the best way of waste reduction is to manage it at source. It is observed that, at the psychological level, waste minimization and characterization share an important connection with recycling, but they depicts two different constructs of waste management behavior. Waste minimization is considered as a separate area of study due to a lower impact of social norms, the noticeable role of habits, and the influence of effortlessness of the task. Demographics had a significant relationship with consumers’ attitude toward waste characterization (Babaei et al., 2015), but the majority of them had inadequate knowledge and practice related to it. As far as household waste minimization behavior is concerned, ‘food waste’ takes an important position in day-to-day decisions. Though it has less visibility to ‘important others’, an emotional component is attached, which leads to the food waste prevention behavior (Quested et al., 2013). This segment of waste has been the focus of research of a considerable number. of articles (Bernstad, 2014; Parizeau et al., 2015; Refsgaard & Magnussen, 2009) in this cluster.

Being the second largest cluster, with 111 articles, it received the first article in 1992. This cluster deals with articles originating from applied social psychology. The core of this cluster deals with the affective factors influencing pro-environmental behaviors like recycling. According to Ouellette and Wood (1998), past behavior could influence future behavior - either through habit formation (while behaving in stable contexts) or through intention formation (less stable contexts). The majority of behaviors are controlled by our habits, due to which we keep doing the task in a routine manner, without much conscious attention (Khan et al., 2019; Olander & Thøgersen, € 1995). There are similar kinds of behaviors with reference to perspective or occurrence or different levels of dedication (easy/difficult), or certain similarities in demographics (Whitmarsh & O’Neill, 2010). These could be grouped to represent a cluster. Spillover refers to the likelihood that the support or performance of an environmental behavior which lead to other pro-environmental behaviors in future (Evans et al., 2013). Research on spillover effects has found that individuals perform similar type of behavior in a regular manner (Nilsson et al., 2017). The spillover effects of these behaviors have also gained attention in this cluster (Thugersen, 1999; Truelove et al., 2016). The anticipated emotions and past behavior are considered to be major drivers of one’s intentions to demonstrate pro-environmental behaviors (Carrus et al., 2008). Resource conservation is affected by social influences, which can therefore be used for bringing about the desired behavior change (Abrahamse & Steg, 2013). Persuasion by campaigners and marketers tries to bring about this change in behavior. Highlighting the role of social identity in shaping one’s motivation to recycle, White et al. (2009) found that personal injunctive norms and descriptive norms were better predictors of intentions to recycle than social injunctive norms. It is hereby evident that this cluster aims to understand the recycling behavior of individuals or communities from multiple perspectives, and thus provides underlying concepts for potential research in this area.

Receiving its first publication in 1997, this cluster is the largest one, containing 151 articles in total. The articles mostly adopt established theories from the literature of psychology, and focus on establishing the associations between the psychological constructs. They investigate different theoretical models of behavior to demonstrate the relationships between determinants and the corresponding behaviors. The most widely used model is that of the Theory of Planned Behavior (TPB), proposed by Ajzen (1985, 1991). According to this theory, an 364 P. R. PHULWANI ET AL. individual’s behavior is guided by beliefs: behavioral, normative and control. These beliefs, in turn, respectively lead to the formation of favorable or unfavorable attitudes toward the behavior in question, subjective norms and perceived behavioral control. Behavioral intentions are determined by these three factors, which, in turn, lead to the manifestation of behavior. In the course of investigating the role of the core constructs of TPB in predicting recycling behavior, various researchers have illustrated the influences of attitude (Ramayah et al., 2012; Tudor et al., 2007), norms (Botetzagias et al., 2015; Park & Ha, 2014; Nigbur et al., 2010) and perceived behavioral control (Hogg et al., 1999; Kraft et al., 2005) on the recycling intentions. These intentions are the key predictors of actual behavior, and hence, they have received a great deal of attention from many researchers due to the convenience of measuring them (through self-reported questionnaires). The intention-behavior gap has been studied by Tudor et al. (2007) and Echegaray and Hansstein (2017). An investigation on antecedent beliefs about recycling activity, such as reduction of the natural resources usage, increase the re-use, and reduce the landfill, helps in identifying enablers and barriers for better proenvironmental behavior (Greaves et al., 2013). Kaiser and Wilson (2004) studied conservation behavior (including recycling) as a goal-directed behavior - ‘something a person does for a subjective reason’. The Model of Goal Directed Behavior (MGB) proposed by Perugini M. & Bagozzi R. P. (2001) is an extended and deeper version of the TPB. It includes constructs like emotions, past behaviors and desires, which mediate or moderate the effects of existing variables on actual behavior. Another important set of theories focusing on normative considerations also gave a clear idea about the other factors which would influence recycling behavior. These studies focused on norms (Norm Activation Theory) and values (Value-Belief-Norm Theory) to understand recycling behavior. Matthies et al. (2012) applied Norm Activation Theory, which emphasizes an individual’s own understanding of moral commitment to do a certain task (Schwartz, 1977). These are activated by the awareness of consequences (AC), which represents the person’s tendency to relate his own behavior to other’s benefit. Ascription of responsibility (AR) is person’s personal feeling of responsibility for the consequences of the behavior (Park & Ha, 2014; Wang et al., 2019). The NAM theory provides the theoretical basis for relationship between these constructs. According to the VBN theory, values (biospheric, altruistic and egoistic) act as antecedents to environmental beliefs (beliefs about AC and AR) which influence personal norms. These personal norms then lead to environmentally significant behavior (Jaini et al., 2020). In terms of recycling behavior, the environmental values play a major role. Research articles in this cluster reveal various relationships among the psychological constructs. Thus, it can be concluded that this cluster focuses on the theoretical frameworks to understand recycling behavior, and that their contribution to the field of RB is indispensible.

Being the smallest cluster with 60 articles, it received the first publication in 1998. The articles in this cluster focus primarily on external factors which had a significant impact on the recycling behavior of individuals and households. Recycling rates are found to be not mere functions of the individual’s psychological system, but greatly driven by external influences (Xu et al., 2017a). While comparing recyclers and non-recyclers, Vining and Ebreo (1990) found that non-recyclers were more affected by convenience and monetary incentives than recyclers were. Convenience relates to the ease of performing a behavior. While considering recycling as the behavior in question, convenience could be associated with the facilitating conditions - like proximity to the collection center, the ease of the process, and less efforts required in terms of time and information search. Convenience was also found to be an important factor in the case of e-waste recycling (Saphores et al., 2006) Financial incentives could stimulate recycling (Miliute-Plepiene et al., 2016). However certain studies found that external incentives (monetary) could destroy intrinsic motivation, and thus, have JOURNAL OF GLOBAL MARKETING 365 a counter-productive effect on recycling (Olander € & Thøgersen, 1995). The cost-benefit analysis of recycling behavior by Berglund (2006) compares the costs and efforts involved in recycling against the return they get by recycling

This cluster has 109 articles, with the first one appearing in 1995. This cluster is interesting because the articles in it contain elaborate research on the recycling behaviors of households or consumers with respect to specific product categories. Rather than focus on the theoretical constructs of attitude-based or value-based models, these articles focus more on the contextual factors that could influence behavior. Packaging waste could be composed of paper, glass, plastic or metal. The differences in their recycling behaviors were studied by Hage et al. (2009), and McDonald and Ball (1998). Due to the nature of fashion, clothing is easily purchased, and swiftly becomes outdated (Joung, 2013). Consumers are ignorant about its recycling (Morgan & Birtwistle, 2009), and disposal mostly occurs either as resale or donations (Shim, 1995). Consumers’ lack of understanding of the consequences of such behavior on the environment, and the influence of environmental attitude on conservation behavior (rather than on waste recycling behavior) were the key findings.

The recycling behavior of waste electrical and electronic equipments has received ample attention from recent researchers. This cluster has 86 articles, beginning in 2006. If we consider recycling of specific product categories, e-waste has received the maximum attention from scholars. E-waste is of grave concern because of the severity of harmful consequences of its inappropriate disposal and generation of large amount e-waste in the last decade. Researchers have studied the impact of psychological and contextual factors on e-waste recycling in their regions e.g., Yin et al. (2014) in China, Song et al. (2012) in Macau, Nnorom et al. (2009) in Nigeria and Araujo et al.   (2012) in Brazil. It is concluded that convenience, habit and benefits seem to play an important role in the recycling of e-waste (Wang et al., 2011). Suitable policies and management, and consumers’ awareness are important pre-requisites for ewaste recycling (Echegaray & Hansstein, 2017). The consumer holds a vital place in the reverse supply chain of electronic equipments (Kumar, 2019) and thus, consumer disposal behavior has been of an area of research interest across various disciplines.
